subject: math
cluster: Use random sampling to draw inferences about a population
intro: When we want to learn about a large group, the population, it is usually impossible to ask everyone. Instead we examine a smaller subset called a sample and use it to make an inference about the whole population. A sample is only trustworthy when it is representative, meaning its makeup mirrors the population. Random sampling, where every member has an equal chance of being chosen, is the most reliable way to get a representative sample. Methods like convenience samples (asking whoever is nearby) and voluntary-response samples (letting people choose to reply) tend to be biased, so generalizations drawn from them may not be valid even when the arithmetic is done correctly.

items.prompt: A principal wants to know the favorite lunch of all $850$ students at a school. She surveys $50$ randomly chosen students. Identify the population and the sample.

steps: The population is the entire group you want to learn about. Here that is all $850$ students at the school.
The sample is the smaller subset you actually examine. Here that is the $50$ students who were surveyed.
Check the relationship: the sample ($50$ students) is part of the larger population ($850$ students), not the other way around.
Because the $50$ students were chosen randomly, the sample has a good chance of being representative of all $850$ students.
solution.answer: Population: all $850$ students at the school. Sample: the $50$ students surveyed.

items.prompt: A reporter interviews the first $20$ people leaving a movie theater to ask what they thought of the film. Classify this sampling method and state whether it is random.

steps: Ask how the people were selected. The reporter simply talked to whoever happened to be leaving first, because they were easy to reach.
Selecting people because they are convenient and nearby is a convenience sample.

In a random sample every member of the population has an equal chance of being chosen. People who left at other times, or who saw a different film, had no chance of being picked, so this is not random.
A convenience sample is not random even though the reporter did not deliberately rig it. Being unplanned is not the same as being random.
solution.answer: It is a convenience sample, and it is not random.

items.prompt: To learn how all city residents commute to work, a researcher surveys only people waiting at a downtown bus stop. Explain why this sample is biased.

steps: The population is all city residents who commute to work.
The sample is made up only of people at a bus stop. These people are far more likely to commute by bus than the average resident.
People who drive, bike, walk, or work from home have little or no chance of being at that bus stop, so they are underrepresented.
Because the sample does not mirror the full range of commuters, it is not representative. This is a source of bias called sampling an unrepresentative subgroup.
Any generalization about how all residents commute, made from this sample, would overstate bus use.
solution.answer: The sample is biased because surveying only people at a bus stop overrepresents bus commuters and leaves out drivers, walkers, and others, so it is not representative of all residents.

items.prompt: A school of $600$ students wants opinions on a new dress code. Three plans are proposed: (1) survey the basketball team, (2) draw $60$ student ID numbers from a hat and survey those students, (3) post the question online and use whoever chooses to reply. Which plan gives the most representative sample, and why?

steps: Plan 1 surveys only the basketball team. That subgroup may share opinions and does not reflect all $600$ students, so it is biased.
Plan 3 lets students decide whether to reply. This is a voluntary-response sample, which tends to attract people with strong opinions and is biased.
Plan 2 draws ID numbers from a hat, so every one of the $600$ students has an equal chance of being selected. That is a simple random sample.
A simple random sample is the most likely to be representative of the whole population, so it supports the most valid inference.
Note that Plan 2 is best because it is random, not because it is easiest. Convenience does not make a sample representative.
solution.answer: Plan 2, drawing ID numbers from a hat, is most representative because it is a simple random sample that gives every student an equal chance of being selected.

items.prompt: From a simple random sample of $40$ of the $500$ books in a library, $10$ are mysteries. A student estimates the total number of mysteries in the library and asks whether the inference is valid. Find the estimate and judge the inference.

steps: Find the proportion of mysteries in the sample: $\frac{10}{40} = \frac{1}{4}$.
Assume the library has the same proportion and scale up to all $500$ books: $\frac{1}{4} \times 500 = 125$.
So a reasonable estimate is about $125$ mystery books.
Now judge validity. The sample was a simple random sample, so every book had an equal chance of being chosen and the sample is likely representative.

Because the sample was random and representative, the inference is valid. The estimate is trustworthy as an approximation, though the actual count could differ slightly due to natural sampling variation.
solution.answer: The estimate is about $125$ mystery books, and the inference is valid because the sample was random and therefore representative.

items.prompt: A factory makes $4000$ light bulbs in a day. A quality inspector tests $80$ bulbs chosen at random. Identify the population and the sample.
items.hint: The population is the whole group you want to know about; the sample is the part you actually examine.

steps: The whole group of interest is all $4000$ bulbs made that day, so that is the population.
The inspector only examined $80$ bulbs, so those $80$ bulbs are the sample.
The sample is a subset of the population.
solution.answer: Population: all $4000$ bulbs made that day. Sample: the $80$ bulbs tested.

items.prompt: A radio host asks listeners to call in and say whether they support a new law. Hundreds of people call. Classify this sampling method and explain whether the large number of callers makes it representative.
items.hint: Think about who decided whether to be in the sample, and whether sample size can fix bias.

steps: Listeners chose for themselves whether to call in, so this is a voluntary-response sample.
Voluntary-response samples attract people with strong opinions, so they tend to be biased.
A large number of callers does not fix this. A big sample that is selected in a biased way is still biased; size does not create representativeness.
Only random selection from the whole population would make the sample representative.
solution.answer: It is a voluntary-response sample. The large number of callers does not make it representative, because a big biased sample is still biased.

items.prompt: A manager wants to know whether all $300$ employees are happy with the cafeteria. She surveys only the employees who eat in the cafeteria every day. Explain the source of bias.
items.hint: Ask which employees had little or no chance of being included.

steps: The population is all $300$ employees.
The sample includes only daily cafeteria eaters, who probably like the cafeteria more than average.
Employees who avoid the cafeteria, perhaps because they dislike it, are left out almost entirely.
Because the sample overrepresents satisfied eaters and underrepresents the unsatisfied, it is not representative. This is bias from sampling an unrepresentative subgroup.
solution.answer: The sample is biased because surveying only daily cafeteria eaters leaves out employees who avoid the cafeteria, so it overstates satisfaction and is not representative of all $300$ employees.

items.prompt: A town of $2000$ registered voters wants to gauge support for a new park. Which plan gives the most representative sample: (A) survey people at the existing park on Saturday, (B) randomly select $150$ names from the official voter list, or (C) survey the mayor's friends? Choose the best plan and explain.
items.hint: Look for the plan that gives every voter an equal chance of being chosen.

steps: Plan A surveys people already at a park, who likely favor parks, so it is a biased convenience sample.
Plan C surveys the mayor's friends, a small unrepresentative subgroup, so it is biased.
Plan B randomly selects names from the full voter list, giving every one of the $2000$ voters an equal chance. That is a simple random sample.
A simple random sample is most likely to be representative, so Plan B is best.
solution.answer: Plan B is best because randomly selecting names from the voter list is a simple random sample that gives every voter an equal chance of being chosen.

items.prompt: In a simple random sample of $50$ of the $1200$ students at a school, $18$ said they walk to school. Estimate how many of the $1200$ students walk to school, and explain whether this inference is valid.
items.hint: Find the sample proportion, scale it up to $1200$, and then check how the sample was selected.

steps: Find the sample proportion of walkers: $\frac{18}{50}$.
Scale up to the full population of $1200$ students: $\frac{18}{50} \times 1200$.
Compute: $\frac{18}{50} \times 1200 = 18 \times 24 = 432$.
So a reasonable estimate is about $432$ students who walk to school.
The sample was a simple random sample, so it is likely representative and the inference is valid, allowing for some natural sampling variation.
solution.answer: About $432$ students walk to school, and the inference is valid because the sample was random and therefore representative.
